title: Should Parents Be Involved in Their Children's Schooling? https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00405841.2022.2096382
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Grolnick and Pomerantz's review of the literature on parental involvement and academic outcomes, which resolves an apparently contradictory evidence base -- some studies show parental involvement helps, others show it harms -- by arguing that type and quality of involvement matter more than involvement per se. Autonomy-supportive, affectively positive involvement tends to help; controlling or affectively negative involvement tends to hurt. Homework assistance in particular is flagged as an area where parental involvement frequently backfires unless it is done constructively, since parental pressure around homework is common and often counterproductive. Barton draws out the practical implications for teachers: build a positive, well-communicated school climate that helps parents feel effective and non-pressured; frame homework-assistance tips as optional strategies rather than directives; and consider redesigning homework toward exploration and process rather than simply correct final answers, which reduces the pressure parents feel to police outcomes.
points: Parental involvement's effect on achievement depends on its type and quality -- autonomy-supportive, positive involvement helps, controlling or negative involvement hurts.
Homework assistance is a particular risk area: parental help with homework frequently backfires unless done constructively.
A positive, well-communicated school climate makes parents more likely to offer autonomy-supportive rather than controlling homework help.
Teachers should frame homework-assistance advice to parents as optional strategies, not directives, to reduce pressure on the family.
quotes: In sum, parent involvement can be a useful and important tool to help facilitate children's academic adjustment. However, consideration must be given to the type of involvement, (e.g., whether parents are assisting with homework or discussing school with children), the quality of involvement (e.g., whether it is autonomy supportive or controlling), and what contributes to the quality of parent involvement
Specifically, assisting with homework is highlighted as an area where parental involvement often negatively impacts students unless done constructively

Focus on fostering positive relationships with parents and creating a positive school climate. When parents perceive a positive school climate with effective communication, they are more likely to provide autonomy and competence support when helping with homework

Communicate with parents about effective homework assistance strategies, framing suggestions in a non-pressuring manner. Teachers can offer tips as strategies that some parents find helpful rather than directives

Reduce pressure on parents and children related to homework. Teachers can move away from traditional homework assignments toward assignments that encourage exploration and emphasize the learning process over the final outcome
